item.title: Assembly Drill 2026-11-25: reverse-function
item.description:
# Reverse-a-function drill — 2026-11-25
Target: Windows x86-64 (arg in `ecx`; return in `eax`).
Reverse this short function to equivalent C. One `test`, two different answers pulled out of the same flags:
```asm mystery: xor eax, eax xor edx, edx test ecx, ecx setg al ; al = 1 if ecx > 0 (signed) setl dl ; dl = 1 if ecx < 0 (signed) sub eax, edx ret ```
What does it return for 42, 0 and -7?
---
## Answer
```c int mystery(int x) { return (x > 0) - (x < 0); } ```
Results: 1, 0 and -1. It's the "sign" function, the same pattern as a branchless qsort comparator `(a > b) - (a < b)`.
## Explanation
- `test ecx, ecx` ANDs ecx with itself just to set flags, so it acts like `cmp ecx, 0`. Both `setg` and `setl` read those flags, and neither changes them, so one test answers two questions. - `setcc` writes only one byte, so eax and edx are zeroed **before** the `test`. Doing it after would wipe the flags, since `xor` sets them. - g/l are the signed conditions (a/b are the unsigned ones). Subtracting the two 0/1 results gives 1, 0 or -1 without a single jump.
